title: Total laryngectomy
text: Total laryngectomy. In this film we follow the operation step by step on a three dimensional model of the larynx and its surroundings: freeing the larynx from above, from the sides and from below, removing it with clear margins, and then rebuilding the pharynx and the airway.

title: Airway and incision
text: If the tumour is obstructing, the airway may need an awake tracheostomy first. An apron incision, U shaped, runs from the mastoid region on each side down to about two finger breadths above the sternal notch. A separate stoma incision is an alternative. Where the stoma will sit is planned from the start.

title: Flaps and strap muscles
text: Subplatysmal flaps are raised, up past the hyoid and down to the clavicles. Any neck dissections are done at this stage. Sternohyoid, sternothyroid and omohyoid are divided low, and kept on the specimen.

title: Thyroid gland
text: The thyroid isthmus is divided. The lobe on the tumour side is removed with the larynx if there is subglottic or transglottic spread. The other lobe is freed off the larynx, keeping its blood supply and its parathyroid glands.

title: Above the hyoid
text: The suprahyoid muscles are cut off the hyoid, staying on the bone, because the hypoglossal nerves and lingual arteries lie just above and lateral to the greater horns. The superior laryngeal pedicles, the artery, vein and internal laryngeal nerve, are found and ligated where they pierce the thyrohyoid membrane.

title: Free the back of the larynx
text: The larynx is rotated, and the inferior constrictor is cut along the back edge of the thyroid lamina. On the side away from the tumour, the mucosa of the piriform fossa is stripped off the inside of the lamina, to keep as much pharyngeal mucosa as possible.

title: Divide the trachea
text: The trachea is cut below the tumour, bevelled so that the back wall is longer, and a sterile tube is passed into the distal trachea for ventilation. The back of the trachea and cricoid is then separated from the oesophagus.

title: Enter the pharynx
text: The pharynx is entered where the tumour is not: through the vallecula above the epiglottis for a glottic or subglottic tumour, or through the opposite piriform fossa. The tumour is inspected, and the larynx is cut free with clear mucosal margins, ending at the postcricoid region.

title: Voice restoration
text: A primary tracheo oesophageal puncture is made through the back wall of the trachea into the oesophagus, for a voice prosthesis. A cricopharyngeal myotomy, or a pharyngeal plexus neurectomy, stops spasm from blocking the voice.

title: Pharyngeal closure
text: The pharynx is closed without tension, in a T or a straight line, with inverting sutures in the mucosa and a second layer of constrictor. A pectoralis major or free flap is used if there is too little mucosa, or if the neck has had radiotherapy.

title: Stoma and closure
text: The trachea is sewn to the skin to make a wide end stoma, and the flaps are closed over drains. After this operation the patient breathes only through the neck, loses the sense of smell, and speaks with a voice prosthesis, oesophageal voice, or an electrolarynx.

title: Structures at risk
text: To summarise, the structures at risk are the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve in the carotid sheath, the remaining thyroid lobe and its parathyroids, and the pharyngeal mucosa needed for a tension free closure. This film is for education only. Always check surgical detail against current atlases and senior guidance.
